title: Entropy microburst field diary
content:
Context:
Personal field diary of recent microburst experiments. Trying to characterize a two-stage arrival pattern that we keep seeing in internal traffic: a small high-amplitude impulse followed by a longer decay tail (looks like a shallow Weibull overlayed on a Poisson spike). Goal: reproduce in harness, measure p50/p95/p99 behavior, and iterate quick mitigations that are low-risk to ship into Dedicated as an experimental flag.

Hypotheses:
- A shallow-coalescing window (~20-60ms) will absorb small impulses without increasing p50 noticeably but should reduce p99 by absorbing queuing oscillations.
- KV-cache warm vs cold interacts nonlinearly with burst shape: cold-cache spikes produce longer service times and thus amplify queue coupling.
- An early-soft-priority lane for tiny requests (<= 64 tokens) will reduce tail for user-visible latencies at low implementation risk.

Test harness and config:
- Model: open-llama-13b-8k-quant (FP16-ish/4-bit emulation for throughput)
- Hardware: single A100-80GB (dev pool), CUDA 12, runtime branch: feature/burst-coalesce (PR 482)
- Inference mode: streaming disabled, single-stream generation, max tokens 256
- Batching: dynamic, max batch 16; coalescing window varied 0, 20, 40, 80 ms
- KV cache states tested: cold (new process per request), warm (cache reused across 10s), seeded (prefetched 1k tokens)
- Arrival generator: composite: Poisson base lambda=25 qps + deterministic spike every 60s (duration 1s) with amplitude +200 rps, plus Weibull noise k=0.9 for the decay tail
- Measurement window: 30 minutes per run, warmup 5 minutes, concurrency probes at client side to maintain target qps
- Observability: server traces (request enqueue time, start service, end service), GPU util metrics (SM util, mem), queue length histograms, and per-token time series saved to /tmp/zetest-run-*.csv

Quick ASCII result summary (p50/p95/p99 in ms, for request-completion time):

coalesce_ms | cache_state | p50  | p95  | p99  | notes
------------|-------------|------|------|------|--------------------------------
0           | cold        | 42   | 210  | 540  | big tails on each spike
20          | cold        | 45   | 180  | 380  | p99 down ~30% vs 0ms
40          | cold        | 48   | 170  | 310  | sweet spot for cold-case
80          | cold        | 60   | 190  | 330  | p50 regresses; batching penalty shows at steady qps
0           | warm        | 38   | 95   | 150  | warm cache dramatically lowers tail
20          | warm        | 40   | 85   | 120  | best overall for warm
40          | warm        | 42   | 92   | 130  | small wins vs 20ms

Observations and qualitative notes:
- Cold-cache case is the pain point: single long service outliers inside the spike create a cascade where the dynamic batching grows and drags overall tail up. Coalescing reduces the number of tiny batches and lets the runtime form medium batches that amortize kernel overhead, which cuts p99 significantly.
- Warm-cache reduces the single-request service time variance; coalescing still helps but with diminishing returns. This is expected: when compute time is predictable, batching only changes queuing shape slightly.
- At 80ms coalescing we start seeing p50 regression at steady load because the coalescing window delays every request, not just the burst arrivals. This shows the classic latency/cost tradeoff.
- GPU metrics: during spike runs with cold cache and no coalescing, SM util spikes to single-core saturation on some kernels (SM 98%) while overall util falls due to kernel serialization; coalescing smoothed the SM util curve and increased sustained throughput.
- Early soft-priority lane for <=64-token requests (provisionally tested by client-side tag and runtime preemption emulation) reduced observed p99 for short requests by ~25% in cold-cache spikes without harming long-running requests. Needs careful fairness checks.

Small diagnostic graphs saved:
- /tmp/zetest-run-20250119-coalesce40-cold.csv -> time,queue_len,service_ms,gpu_sm
- /tmp/zetest-run-20250119-coalesce0-warm.csv -> ...
(These CSVs are too big to paste here; aggregated stats above.)

Immediate conclusions and recommendations:
1) Ship a small-server-experiment flag: coalescing-window default 20ms for cold-cache paths only (toggle per-model). This gives most p99 benefit with minimal p50 regression.
2) Add a cached-warmup hint in client SDKs: if a request is likely to hit cold cache (new conversation, long prefix), optionally set "low-latency":true so server can use soft-priority lane. This is an opt-in telemetry + SDK change.
3) Run fairness test matrix before broader rollout: mixed client mix (short vs long requests) at steady qps to ensure large-batch throughput isn't starved.
4) Instrument per-token service variance more thoroughly (histograms by token index) — current traces hint that early tokens in generation are the expensive ones in cold cache.

To-do (next runs):
- Repeat the 40ms cold run with model quant-slice enabled (we suspect quant path has different kernel scheduling behavior).
- Add jitter to spike timing to avoid synchronized client-side bursts (test whether real-world timing jitter reduces worst-case tail).
- Run a 6-hour soak with coalesce=20ms warm/cold toggling to capture low-frequency events.
- Write a short runbook entry for on-call describing quick mitigation (flip coalesce flag per pool + emergency rollback steps).

Notes to self:
- Save the small priority lane prototype code as patch that can be toggled per endpoint (easy rollback).
- Talk to Riley about adding a lightweight telemetry flag for "likely-cold-cache" from the SDK; keep privacy-preserving (no conversation text sent, just boolean hint).
- Present this in next Tuesday runtime sync (5 minutes + demo of CSVs).

Rough action timeline:
- Today: land PR with added coalescing flag and basic metrics hooks (pr:482 incremental).
- +2 days: run extended soak and include fairness matrix.
- +1 week: propose default for Dedicated experimental pools and document rollback plan.

End of entry.

-- Zeke T. (scratch notes; do not file as official artifact yet)
